title: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors Used Concomitantly with Insulin Secretagogues and the Risk of Serious Hypoglycemia
authors: Hee Nam Y, Brensinger CM, Bilker WB, Flory JH, Leonard CE, Hennessy S
population: Self-controlled case series of patients with serious hypoglycaemia (hospital or emergency presentation) during insulin secretagogue or metformin treatment, in Medicaid claims from 5 US states linked to Medicare
funder: This study was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK102694, R01AG025152, R01AG060975, R01AG064589, R01DA048001) and the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (CER-2017C3-9230). These organizations had no role in the design and conduct of the study, data collection and analysis, interpretation of the results, writing and review of the manuscript, or the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.
authorConflicts: The University of Pennsylvania Center for Pharmacoepidemiology Research and Training, directed by Hennessy, receives funds from Pfizer and Sanofi for education; Hennessy has received support through his employer from Pfizer, Sanofi and Johnson and Johnson and consulted for Merck, the Medullary Thyroid Cancer Consortium and Eli Lilly, all stated as unrelated.
result: Rate ratios of serious hypoglycaemia during ACE-inhibitor-exposed against unexposed time: glipizide 1.06 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.15), glyburide 1.05 (0.96 to 1.15), repaglinide 1.15 (0.94 to 1.41), metformin as negative control 1.02 (0.97 to 1.06), glimepiride 1.23 (1.11 to 1.37) and nateglinide 0.73 (0.56 to 0.96). The authors conclude that the overall pattern does not suggest increased serious hypoglycaemia, with the possible exception of glimepiride.
